title: Νυκτερὶς καὶ βάτος καὶ αἴθυια
titleEn: The Bat, the Bramble and the Shearwater
part: The Bat, the Bramble and the Shearwater (Chambry 250 · Perry 171)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 250 (= Perry 171). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Νυκτερὶς καὶ βάτος καὶ αἴθυια ἑταιρείαν ποιησάμεναι, ἐμπορικὸν διέγνωσαν βίον ζῆν.
sentences.tr: Nykteris kai batos kai aithyia hetaireian poiēsamenai, emporikon diegnōsan bion zēn.
sentences.l: A bat and a bramble and a shearwater, having made a partnership, resolved to live a merchant's life.
sentences.n: ἑταιρεία is an association of partners, and here a trading company: the three put in capital, goods and cargo and share the voyage. αἴθυια is a diving sea-bird, glossed in the older lexicons as the shearwater; the ancient identification is not certain, and the fable needs only that it dives and haunts the shore. It is not the gull, which is λάρος (fable 193). All three nouns are feminine, so the participle ποιησάμεναι is feminine plural.

sentences.t: Ἡ μὲν οὖν νυκτερὶς ἀργύριον δανεισαμένη καθῆκεν εἰς τὸ μέσον, ἡ δὲ βάτος ἐσθῆτα μετ’ ἑαυτῆς ἔλαβεν, ἡ δὲ αἴθυια τρίτη χαλκόν· καὶ ἀπέπλευσαν.
sentences.tr: Hē men oun nykteris argyrion daneisamenē kathēken eis to meson, hē de batos esthēta met’ heautēs elaben, hē de aithyia tritē chalkon· kai apepleusan.
sentences.l: The bat, then, having borrowed silver, put it down into the common stock; the bramble took clothing along with herself; and the shearwater, third, bronze; and they sailed away.
sentences.i: So the bat borrowed money and laid it into the common fund, the bramble brought clothing with her, and the shearwater, the third of them, bronze; and they set sail.
sentences.n: δανείζω in the active is 'to lend', in the middle 'to borrow' — the bat's capital is not her own, which is why the creditors are waiting for her at the end. εἰς τὸ μέσον, 'into the midst', is the standing phrase for a common fund. μέν … δέ … δέ sets out the three partners one after another.

sentences.t: Χειμῶνος δὲ σφοδροῦ γενομένου καὶ τῆς νεὼς περιτραπείσης, πάντα ἀπολέσασαι αὐταὶ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν διεσώθησαν.
sentences.tr: Cheimōnos de sphodrou genomenou kai tēs neōs peritrapeisēs, panta apolesasai autai epi tēn gēn diesōthēsan.
sentences.l: But a fierce storm having arisen and the ship having been overturned, having lost everything they themselves were brought safe to land.
sentences.i: But a fierce storm came on and the ship went over, and though they lost everything, they themselves got safe to shore.
sentences.n: νεώς is the Attic genitive of ναῦς. Two genitive absolutes in a row carry the whole wreck, and only then does the main verb arrive. διεσώθησαν is an aorist passive used intransitively, 'they came safe through' — the same shape as ἀπηλλάγη at fable 249, where English has a plain active.

sentences.t: Ἐξ ἐκείνου τοίνυν ἡ μὲν αἴθυια τοῖς αἰγιαλοῖς ἀεὶ παρεδρεύει, μή που τὸν χαλκὸν ἐκβάλλῃ ἡ θάλαττα· ἡ δὲ νυκτερὶς τοὺς δανειστὰς φοβουμένη, τῆς μὲν ἡμέρας οὐ φαίνεται, νύκτωρ δ’ ἐπὶ νομὴν ἔξεισιν· ἡ δὲ βάτος τῆς τῶν παριόντων ἐσθῆτος ἐπιλαμβάνεται, εἴ που τὴν οἰκείαν ἐπιγνοίη ζητοῦσα.
sentences.tr: Ex ekeinou toinyn hē men aithyia tois aigialois aei paredreuei, mē pou ton chalkon ekballēi hē thalatta· hē de nykteris tous daneistas phoboumenē, tēs men hēmeras ou phainetai, nyktōr d’ epi nomēn exeisin· hē de batos tēs tōn pariontōn esthētos epilambanetai, ei pou tēn oikeian epignoiē zētousa.
sentences.l: From that time, accordingly, the shearwater sits always beside the beaches, in case the sea should somewhere cast the bronze up; and the bat, fearing her creditors, is not seen by day, but goes out by night to feed; and the bramble lays hold of the clothing of those passing by, on the chance that, searching, she should somewhere recognize her own.
sentences.i: Ever since, the shearwater keeps watch along the beaches, in case the sea should throw the bronze up somewhere; the bat, afraid of her creditors, is not seen by day but goes out at night to feed; and the bramble catches at the clothes of passers-by, searching on the chance of knowing her own again.
sentences.n: The close is aetiological: the fable ends by telling why each creature still behaves as it does. μή που with the subjunctive after a verb of watching is the regular clause of apprehension, 'in case…', and εἴ που with the optative is its counterpart in a clause of hope. παρεδρεύω is to sit constantly beside a thing, the word used of an attendant at a post. τῆς ἡμέρας is a genitive of time within which, 'in the course of the day'. ἐπιλαμβάνομαι takes the genitive of what it seizes.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι περὶ ἃ σπουδάζομεν, τούτοις ἐς ὕστερον περιπίπτομεν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti peri ha spoudazomen, toutois es hysteron peripiptomen.
sentences.l: The fable shows that the things about which we take pains, with these we afterwards fall in.
sentences.i: The fable shows that we end by running up against the very things we busied ourselves with.
sentences.n: The relative clause comes first and is then gathered up by the demonstrative τούτοις — a very common Greek shape where English would keep the relative inside. περιπίπτω takes the dative of what one falls in with, and it is nearly always something one would rather not meet, as of the sick man's flux at fable 249.
